summary:
Amazonas stands under Brazil's national framework: marriage, legal gender recognition, hate-crime criminalisation and medical regulation are set nationally, and the national record carries those provisions. The state's own layer is narrow. State Ordinary Law No. 3079 of 12 September 2006 prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity across employment, housing and other areas, and a state provision in force since 2 August 2006 prohibits the manufacture, sale and distribution of symbols inciting discrimination, prejudice, hatred or violence on gender-identity grounds. Sexual orientation has been covered by state anti-discrimination policy since 2006 as well.

Restroom access in Manaus is restricted by municipal law: the mayor signed a measure on 18 October 2022 banning multi-gender or unisex restrooms in the city. The state has no explicit statutory protection for restroom or facility access on gender-identity grounds.

Non-binary recognition has no state framework. Amazonas has no law recognising a non-binary gender, and treatment has been case-by-case since April 2022. In 2022 a resident became the first non-binary person in the state to obtain recognition: the rectification was completed in Rio de Janeiro and applied in Manaus only after the Amazonas Public Defenders Office intervened, because the state's registry offices held no gender-neutral marker.

Gender-affirming care for minors is prohibited in the state: the governor signed Law 7552 on 10 June 2025 banning it for people under 18. Adult access to trans health care is contested rather than settled. On 1 November 2023 the Public Defenders Office health unit opened a collective procedure on public health system access covering hormone therapy, outpatient services and the absence of authorisation for transition surgeries, and in August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutors Office recommended that Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital transition services, including sexual reassignment surgery, with deadlines for approval and presentation to the Ministry of Health.

Violence against LGBTQ people in the state is recorded poorly. The Brazilian Public Security Forum reports a rise in registered cases and a total of 43 cases. That is a raw count with no population denominator, and it cannot show trans-specific risk on its own. Research on 2021 to 2022 records in the capital and the interior found that crimes involving homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual victims were 0.36 per cent of all reports, that homophobia and transphobia motives and the gender, sexuality and race categories were not identified in the records, that victims were at times recorded as perpetrators because of failures in police occurrence reports, and that public agents were unprepared to handle these cases. No separate figures for transgender victims are available.

On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults; residents told reporters he had previously been bullied by other young people in the area. The killing is documented as homophobic. The source states no disaggregation for transgender victims in that case and gives no general homicide rate for the state, so no comparison against the background rate can be made.
tangentialFactors:
The state legislature has moved against expression and youth participation. Ordinary Law No. 6469 of 2023 bars children and adolescents from taking part in pride parades, with fines of up to 10,000 reais for non-compliance. On 17 October 2024 the Legislative Assembly enacted a law prohibiting the reproduction of digital media involving children linked to homosexuality; on 13 December 2025 that law was amended to remove the term homosexuality and to prohibit instead the reproduction of sexual content involving children in cultural and artistic media. Ordinary Law No. 6463 of 10 October 2023 prohibits the use of neutral language, non-binary dialect or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in the curricula and teaching materials of public and private schools, and in official documents of educational institutions and public agencies across the state.

Recognition for non-binary people in Amazonas depends on procedures completed elsewhere and on local intervention. The 2022 case required rectification in Rio de Janeiro followed by action by the Amazonas Public Defenders Office in Manaus, and no gender-neutral marker has been available at the state's registry offices.
localsOnly:
State institutions have built a trans-specific service and oversight layer. In 2021 the Amazonas Public Defenders Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group, which works on human rights violations and trains security agents. Its health unit, Nudesa, opened a collective preparatory procedure on 1 November 2023 to enforce public health system access for trans people, covering hormone therapy, outpatient services and the lack of authorisation for transition surgeries including sexual reassignment. After a meeting in October 2023, Manaus municipal health officials committed to dispensing standardised hormone medications on prescriptions issued by the Ambulatorio Codajas and to designating reference primary-care units in each zone of the city, while the state health secretariat was required to report on gaps in equitable care and hormone therapy.

In August 2024 the Amazonas Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right for LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents expelled from their homes, setting out the protections owed to them and stating that conversion therapies are prohibited and ineffective, with legal support available through the Specialised Human Rights Public Defender's Office.

Family recognition in the state was granted by a state court before the national framework settled: in November 2012 a judge of the Amazonas Court of Justice authorised the first adoption by a same-sex couple in Amazonas.
outOfScopeNotes:
Outcomes for the state's enforcement machinery are unresolved. The inventory does not record whether Amazonas met the Federal Public Prosecutors Office's August 2024 deadlines for enabling outpatient and hospital transition services, nor the result of the Public Defenders Office procedure opened in November 2023. Whether the 2023 law barring minors from pride parades and the 2024 media law have been enforced, and through how many penalties, is not stated.

State-level figures are incomplete. The 59 per cent rise in registry gender changes reported by 2024 is not attributed specifically to Amazonas, so the state's share is not sourced. The 43 registered LGBTQ violence cases carry no population denominator, and the cited research describes the underlying records as under-reporting and misclassifying victims, so the figure is a floor rather than a measure of magnitude. No trans-disaggregated violence data for Amazonas were located, and the sources contain no documented assessment of societal tolerance of transgender people in the state.
